title: The Ending: The A-Level Exam and Christopher's Question
description: The resolution of the play: Christopher sits his A-level Maths exam, Reverend Peters invigilation,.
content_html:
Resolution: The A-Level Mathematics Exam

After returning to Swindon from London, Christopher's primary goal is to sit his A-level Mathematics exam. This matters intensely: Siobhan had told him he would be able to take it, but the disruption of his journey to London and the breakdown of his home life has thrown everything into uncertainty. The A-level exam represents more than academic achievement — it is proof that despite everything that has happened, Christopher can still function, still achieve, still be himself.

In Simon Stephens's play, the A-level exam is staged literally: Christopher sits down to take it onstage, with Reverend Peters (the school's vicar and invigilator) presiding over the examination. The audience watches Christopher work through a complex mathematical problem in real time. This is a bold theatrical choice: the play slows down to let mathematics take centre stage. Christopher achieves an A*.

Key Fact

The A-level Mathematics exam is staged literally onstage, with Reverend Peters as invigilator. Christopher sits the exam and achieves an A*. In the novel, this is narrated in prose — in Stephens's play, the audience watches it happen.

The Post-Curtain Maths Scene

One of the most distinctive features of Stephens's play-text is what happens after the main action concludes. After the curtain call, Christopher returns to the stage to solve his favourite question from the A-level Mathematics paper. This is a full, staged, theatrical event: music, lighting, mathematical projections, and — in some productions — confetti. The audience watches Christopher work through the problem with complete focus and joy.

This post-curtain maths sequence is unique to the play-text. It has no equivalent in Haddon's novel, which merely narrates the A-level exam result in prose. Stephens's choice to stage the mathematics as a performance transforms it into a celebration: not just of Christopher's intelligence, but of his way of engaging with the world. The theatrical staging treats mathematical problem-solving as something worth watching — as a form of beauty and competence as stageable as any other art form.

In Haddon's novel, there is a mathematical appendix printed at the back — a full proof that the reader can engage with as text. Stephens cannot reproduce a printed appendix on stage. Instead, he stages the mathematics as a live event: Christopher works through the problem in front of the audience, with theatrical support from the lighting, projections, and music. The effect is to show mathematics as Christopher experiences it — not as a dry academic exercise but as a place of clarity, certainty, and delight. Christopher says: 'Prime numbers are what is left when you have taken all the patterns away.' Mathematics is what remains when the noise of human confusion is removed — pure, reliable, beautiful. The post-curtain scene is a theatrical embodiment of that idea.

Christopher's Question: The Play's Final Lines

The play's ending is fundamentally different from the novel's — and this difference is crucial for Eduqas students. In Haddon's novel, Christopher makes a declarative statement: 'And I know I can do this because I went to London on my own, and because I solved the mystery of Who Killed Wellington? And I found my mother and I was brave and I wrote a book and that means I can do anything.'

In Stephens's play, this becomes a question addressed directly to Siobhan: 'Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?' This is a fundamental change. The novel's Christopher arrives at declarative certainty through a chain of reasoning: because I did these things, I can do anything. The play's Christopher arrives at the same point but frames it as an open question to his teacher. He needs Siobhan to confirm what he is beginning to believe about himself.

Key Fact

The play ends with Christopher asking Siobhan: 'Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?' — a question. The novel ends with Christopher declaring 'I can do anything' — a statement. This tonal difference (aspiration vs certainty, question vs declaration) is one of the most important distinctions between the two texts. Never quote the novel's declarative ending in the Eduqas exam.

The Significance of the Question Form

The shift from declarative to interrogative is a significant theatrical and thematic choice by Stephens. By ending on a question, the play creates a more open, uncertain, and aspirational ending than the novel. Christopher has not arrived at full confidence — he is reaching for it, through Siobhan. He needs his teacher's validation of what he is beginning to sense about himself.

This ending reinforces Siobhan's function throughout the play. She is not just a narrator — she is the person Christopher most trusts to tell him the truth about himself. The question 'Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?' is directed at the one person who has consistently given him honest, accurate information about what is possible. Her potential answer is the last image the play offers: not certainty, but the opening of possibility.

For AO2 analysis, the question form is important: a question requires a response, whereas a declaration does not. By ending the play on an unanswered question, Stephens leaves the audience in the same position as Christopher — waiting for a confirmation that feels within reach but has not quite arrived. It is an emotionally open ending that treats the audience as participants rather than spectators.

Reverend Peters — the school's vicar — invigilates Christopher's A-level exam. His presence is more than logistical: he represents the institutional framework within which Christopher's achievement is validated. An A-level examination is a formal, public event; its result is certified and witnessed. By staging the exam with Reverend Peters present, Stephens creates a theatrical scene in which Christopher's intelligence is not just experienced privately but witnessed institutionally. The A* is not just something Christopher knows about himself — it is recognised by the structures of the world beyond his family.

The Arc of the Play: From Wellington to the A*

The play's two-act structure moves from a death — Wellington's murder — to a proof: Christopher's A-level result. The detective plot (who killed Wellington?) resolves into something much larger: who is Christopher, and what can he achieve? The answer is given not through dialogue but through theatrical action: a fifteen-year-old autistic boy, whose father lied to him, whose mother left, who travelled to London alone through overwhelming sensory chaos, sits an A-level Mathematics paper and achieves the highest possible result. Then he asks his teacher whether that means he can do anything.

Stephens's ending resists the false comfort of total resolution. Christopher and Ed are tentatively rebuilding their relationship. Christopher lives partly with Judy, partly with Ed. The family is not restored. But Christopher himself has expanded: he has discovered what he can do alone, in the world, when the need arises. The question to Siobhan is therefore not doubt — it is the first articulation of a new self-understanding.

Effective drama analysis requires attention to stagecraft — considering not just what happens but how the playwright shapes the audience's response through every element of performance and text. In your exam response, identify specific techniques and explain their effect precisely.

exam_tip_html: The ending is one of the most frequently examined aspects of the play. Be precise about the play's ending — Christopher asks Siobhan a question ('Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?'), not the novel's declarative 'I can do anything'. Also discuss the post-curtain maths scene as a theatrical device unique to the play: it stages mathematics as a performance, transforming what Haddon printed as an appendix into a live theatrical event. Both of these are excellent AO2 points about form and Stephens's adaptation choices.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Christopher sits his A-level Maths exam onstage and achieves an A*. Reverend Peters invigilates. This is staged, not narrated.
  • After the curtain call, Christopher returns to solve his favourite maths problem in a theatrical event with music, lights, and projections — unique to the play-text.
  • The play ends with Christopher asking Siobhan 'Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?' — a question, not the novel's declarative 'I can do anything'. This is a crucial distinction for the Eduqas exam.

practice_questions.text: How does Stephens use the ending of the play to explore the theme of independence and achievement?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of the ending as the culmination of Christopher's journey. Discusses: the A-level exam staged literally, the post-curtain maths scene as a theatrical celebration, and the question to Siobhan as the first articulation of a new self-understanding. Connects ending to the journey to London (Acts 1-2) as the evidence base for Christopher's question. AO2: question vs declarative form — what the shift means theatrically.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis with range and evidence.
Mid band (15-21): Explained response.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Some points about the ending.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Stephens present mathematics as significant to Christopher's identity and to the play's meaning?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of mathematics as Christopher's language of certainty. Discusses: prime numbers as 'what is left when you have taken all the patterns away', the post-curtain maths scene as theatrical celebration of his mode of understanding, the A-level exam as public validation. AO2: how Stephens stages mathematics (projections, lighting, ensemble) vs how Haddon prints it (mathematical appendix). AO4: the theatrical choice to perform mathematics.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis with evidence.
Mid band (15-21): Some relevant points.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Basic discussion.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: Explore the significance of Siobhan's role in the play's final scene.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of Siobhan at the end. Discusses: her dual role as teacher and narrator converging in the final moment (Christopher asks his teacher the question she has narrated him building towards), the significance of the question form (needing her confirmation), and what this reveals about trust and relationship. Range: traces Siobhan from Act 1 (encouraging the book) to the final question.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis with range.
Mid band (15-21): Explained response.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Some points.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Stephens uses the ending of the play to the ending of Haddon's novel. What does the change from declaration to question achieve?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of the adaptation choice. Novel: declarative statement ('I can do anything') — certainty arrived at through a chain of reasoning, Christopher as sole narrator concluding his own story. Play: question to Siobhan ('Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?') — aspiration rather than certainty, Christopher needing his teacher's confirmation. What does each ending say about independence, confidence, and the need for relationship? AO4: Stephens's adaptation choices.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear comparison with evidence.
Mid band (15-21): Some engagement with the distinction.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Basic points.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Stephens use the post-curtain maths scene to convey ideas about Christopher and about theatrical form?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of the post-curtain scene as theatrical choice. Discusses: what it communicates about Christopher (his joy in mathematical precision, his connection to clarity and certainty), how it transforms Haddon's printed appendix into a live performance, what it says about the play's attitude to different modes of intelligence. AO2: how staging choices create meaning.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis with theatrical awareness.
Mid band (15-21): Some relevant points.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Basic discussion.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does the structure of the play — from Wellington's death to Christopher's A* — create meaning?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive structural analysis. Discusses: the movement from a death (investigation, crisis, disruption) to a proof (exam, achievement, question). The detective plot resolving into a question about personal capability. Act 1's domestic stability → Act 2's chaos → the ending's tentative new beginning. AO2: structural choices — two-act form, the theatrical arc from crime to achievement.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear structural analysis.
Mid band (15-21): Some engagement with structure.

flashcard_questions.q: What are Christopher's final words in Stephens's play?
flashcard_questions.a: 'Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?' — a question to his teacher, not a declaration.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the play's ending differ from the novel's ending?
flashcard_questions.a: The novel ends with Christopher declaring 'I can do anything' (certainty). The play ends with Christopher asking Siobhan 'Does that mean I can do anything?' (aspiration/question).

flashcard_questions.q: What happens after the curtain call in Stephens's play?
flashcard_questions.a: Christopher returns to stage to solve his favourite maths problem from the A-level paper — staged with music, lights, and projections as a theatrical celebration.

flashcard_questions.q: Who is Reverend Peters and what is his role in the ending?
flashcard_questions.a: The school's vicar who invigilates Christopher's A-level Mathematics exam onstage — his presence provides institutional validation of Christopher's achievement.

flashcard_questions.q: What result does Christopher achieve in his A-level Mathematics exam?
What is the significance of ending on a question rather than a declaration?
flashcard_questions.a: It creates an open, aspirational ending. Christopher has not arrived at certainty — he is reaching for it, needing Siobhan's confirmation. The audience is left waiting alongside him.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the prime numbers quote and what does it reveal about Christopher?
flashcard_questions.a: 'Prime numbers are what is left when you have taken all the patterns away.' Mathematics is Christopher's language of certainty — a space of clarity when human confusion is removed.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Stephens's staging of the maths exam differ from Haddon's treatment of it in the novel?
flashcard_questions.a: Haddon narrates the exam result in prose and includes a mathematical appendix. Stephens stages the exam literally onstage, with Reverend Peters invigilating, and adds the post-curtain scene as.

glossary_terms.definition: A sentence that states a fact or makes an assertion — using a full stop rather than a question mark. The novel's ending uses a declarative; the play uses a question.
A sentence that asks a question — the form Stephens uses for Christopher's final line, creating an open, aspirational ending rather than the novel's certainty.
A person who supervises an examination — Reverend Peters invigilates Christopher's A-level Maths exam onstage.

A theatrical scene that occurs after the main action has ended and the curtain has been taken — in this play, Christopher returns to solve his favourite maths problem in a musical, theatrical celebration.
The overall shape of a play's action — here, from Wellington's death (Act 1) to Christopher's A* and question (the ending), tracing a journey from crisis to achievement.
The playwright's use of dramatic techniques including staging, lighting, dialogue, and structure to create meaning.
The sense of anticipation or unease created by conflict, uncertainty, or approaching crisis in drama.
